#68. Is High-Gloss Tile Really That Slippery On A Bathroom Floor?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 25m • 📚 Deep Dive (5025 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Stylebyemilyhenderson ↗ Open Full Page

Is High-Gloss Tile Really That Slippery On A Bathroom Floor?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5025 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Stylebyemilyhenderson

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that pinterest is the “Tinder” of design dating apps.
  • Sources indicate that I wrote about wanting a higher-gloss tile finish to contrast against all the rustic texture a couple of weeks ago when two commenters warned me not to do it.
  • But as I was finally ready to make the decision, I really thought about the cons of this as flooring:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that pinterest is the “Tinder” of design dating apps. You think you have what you need and love, something that checks most of your boxes, and then you’re scrolling and you see a fresh shiny (literally) thing that makes you wonder if it could be even better. I finally have a tiny bit of brain space (and I do mean tiny) to start back into the guest cottage design process, namely the bathroom that has been at a standstill awaiting my flooring decision. I had it all locked in- thin-set brick in a herringbone pattern. I sampled a ton, made my decision, and ordered a box. I was about to order the rest, but as the wood on the walls went in, I realized that this bathroom is going to lean VERY rustic, with a lot of dark reddish tones on all walls, ceilings, AND the floor. And while I like rustic in theory, and nothing is wrong with leaning into a vibe, I had second thoughts that turned into a U-turn. Are we missing an opportunity to do something spectacular and extra beautiful??? I know that the brick will look good, but could something else look even better?

Sources indicate that I wrote about wanting a higher-gloss tile finish to contrast against all the rustic texture a couple of weeks ago when two commenters warned me not to do it. And I listened. One said they were in the middle of tearing out their high-gloss tile as we speak. OOF. Now I have a feeling the tile is a large-scale 12×24 porcelain situation that a lot of builders put in (because it’s affordable to buy and install) and it’s 100% too slippery for a floor. When I took to Reddit, this was the case – all significant-format tile complaints. Sure, the polished high-gloss doesn’t help, but I wonder if it’s more the lack of texture on the tile or grout lines that makes it specifically slippery. Ceramic tile doesn’t come that big, but if it did, I wonder if it would be almost as slippery. So let’s go through the pros and cons of bathroom tile flooring, what we are considering, and then I’d LOVE to hear any warnings about high-gloss tile.

Look how good it was going to look. I chose this for 3 main reasons.

But as I was finally ready to make the decision, I really thought about the cons of this as flooring:.

While it’s not totally off the table, I’m starting to see all these gorgeous high-gloss tile floors in kitchens and bathrooms, and while I know intellectually that it’s not recommended, I just think contrasting off the reclaimed wood on the walls would be STUNNING.

Industry observers note that and then Karen and Kim in the comments reminded me of the slippery factor, and I don’t like tile regrets. And while I think most people would be fine, the facts are that this bathroom is a portal from the backyard into the game room, with kids in the summer on the grass with wet feet flying through to go to the bathroom or play Pop-a-Shot. And then if and when anybody who was older were to live here, I would worry about it as well.

But then there are a lot of things that are “against the rules” when really it’s not that big of a deal. Unlacquered brass plumbing is one of them (the patina can go to tarnish really quickly if you don’t take care of it). Real wood kitchen islands are another (we have a lot of wear and tear on ours and I have zero regrets). TV above a fireplace is so controversial (but I’ve done it and love it!). Now neither of these things are “dangerous,” but I also wondered if having enough grout lines and a slight texture would solve this particular problem.

I used 2×2 high gloss tile flooring in our kids’ bathroom at the mountain house, and it was never slippery. In fact, you would think that it would be hard on your feet since zellige can be irregular, but we didn’t notice anything at all. Zero regrets.

Here we used a 1×2 herringbone, high gloss on mesh sheets, and zero slip challenges. This is likely because of the amount of grout lines that inhibit slippage. The vintage rug also helps. But this guest cottage bathroom is big, and so I love the idea of scaling up the tile a little bit more (this just feels too small to me).

Sources indicate that now this is the scale I was thinking for the guest cottage bathroom, but not matte. This tile works so great because it is the Pratt and Larsen brownstone finish that inherently has a lot of texture PLUS, there are still grout lines. While I’m sure that if we had water all over the tile and someone was running barefoot from the outside, they could slip. For the most part, we’ve had zero challenges with this.

Industry observers note that this bathroom was bigger, with more floor space, so I liked the idea of scaling up. I LOVE this choice for in here and would do it again in this same vibe for sure. The natural stone texture made it inherently non-slip even though it was large-scale, with few grout lines. I suppose I could consider this – definitely softer on the foot than brick…like a little boring and safe, but worth exploring. But no, it’s just too harsh and dark for this vibe.

Recent findings suggest that here we really lived on the edge of danger by installing a polished stone slab, cut into 12″ square “tiles”. Y’all, ZERO SLIPPAGE. Why? Bath mat (not shown, lol). And in the guest cottage I will have a vintage runner near the door, then a smaller rug between the sink and the water closet (and a bath mat outside the shower). So maybe rugs are the answer?

As I was writing this post, I was like, “wait, what did we put in Ken’s bathroom?” and with a quick Google search I was reminded that I DID use a 12×24 honed marble tile on their bathroom floor, outside of the tub/shower area. I texted them asking about it and got this immediately in return: “It’s great! Not slippery. No problems at all”. So large scale is fine if matte, high-gloss tile in small scale is fine, but what about in the middle??

Industry observers note that I love the scale of the mudroom tile (and the border), which made me wonder if we did the same scale, but just with a slight sheen to it (doesn’t have to be high gloss), something to contrast with the rustic walls and pop off in a cool way…could that work? So this one is more of a crowdsourcing situation. As a reminder:.

It has been revealed that it’s not like my heart is so set on high-gloss tile that I’m willing to endanger the children or seniors in my life, but I also don’t want to make decisions based on a couple of anecdotal stories with the extreme examples that I found on the internet (i.e., 12×24 porcelain sheet tile). At the same time, I also REALLY, REALLY, REALLY don’t like taking risks with tile because it’s one of the most permanent fixtures in your house, so once these go in, they are not coming out in my lifetime. I have that mantra “simple but special” for permanent fixtures (tile, flooring, plumbing, millwork), which I remarked so often one year that it became a drinking game, but it’s true – and I love the hell out of all of my tile choices (the only regret was the cement tile on the floor – DON’T DO IT INSIDE).

Yesterday I popped into Ann Sacks and asked them about floor tile, and they agreed with me that it’s mostly about grout lines. They showed me a tile finish, Provencal, that we LOVED. It’s shown in the lighter blue above. It’s actually on the less expensive side and has a slightly imperfect texture that I think works really well with the old-world vibe of the house, but we can get in a lot of colors (I’m obsessed with that blue on the right).

So now I’m leaning towards the texture on the left (in a 3×8 herringbone + border) in the color on the right. Add some rugs, and I think we are safe.

Industry observers note that but please, sound off here if you have experience with really slippery tile floors. If so, and you have a second, attach a photo to the comment so we can see what to avoid. I need to know if it’s a design urban legend (like the importance of the “kitchen triangle,” which is all just actually a preference), or if it’s mostly just these high-gloss 12×24 large format tiles, OR if putting in a 3×8 texture semi-gloss herringbone floor would work. Per my book, I do love a design rule, but I also really, really, really like breaking them if I do it thoughtfully and intentionally. They can pay off, but the risks can be so high….

Opening Image Credit: Photo by Kaitlin Green.

Have you thought about using a product that relates to your outdoor pool deck/walkways? If I understand the brief for this room, I think both slippery tiles and dirt are of concern. Your tile grout getting dirty may be something to consider. If there is a lot of outdoor traffic coming through this space, relying on rugs alone might not do the trick. You’ve sampled a lot of “indoor” products – but I think the function of this room might warrant more outdoor products.

According to recent reports, in this vein, why not just use the same type of tile that’s in the mudroom, with the color of your choice? Seems to me it relates to the indoor/outdoor wear element the best, and you already love it.

It has been revealed that yes! both great ideas. I’m not as excited about a blue stone or outdoor slate tile, but I know its a fantastic function. I love the mudroom tile, just hoping for a little more sheen. We’ll see xx.

According to recent reports, I don’t think it’s that massive of a deal to clean. I love the blue tile you found at Ann Sacks. Go for it.

I’d be worried about a glazed tile getting scratched or chipped by people coming in from outside with shoes with a pebble stuck in the sole. I think a natural stone in a smaller scale, herringbone tile pattern would be better. I don’t know, the glazed ceramic tile just doesn’t seem to jive in here for me.

Sources indicate that I think the lighter blue would be better than the darker, if the intention is to lighten things up a bit. it might also draw out some of the lighter tones in the wood. I also think the slate or some other natural stone (not marble) would be lovely and reflective of the period and rooms like that that are bridges between outside and inside. never been a fan of herringbone tile, but what a boring world it would be if everybody had the same taste!

Recent findings suggest that question: this room is having a tub in it, is that right? what are the window treatments going to be? that’s a huuuuuge window for a ground floor bathroom! beautiful, but gotta cover it up sometimes!

I was wondering about the comfort of being naked with that window too! I think I’m not quite understanding this room. I remember mention of a urinal. Is that going in the internal structure with the toilet? I would have thought a male standing to pee is the bathroom activity that requires the least amount of privacy and time compared to anything else a bathroom is used for, so I’d put it out in the open without any extra doors to be slowing down the function of something that is designed to speed things up!

As for the tile, I have large ceramic tiles in my kitchen, that leads straight from the garden, and they have been perfectly fine for years in terms of slippage, robustness and ease of cleaning. They are a more matte finish.

hiya. good to know about your tile! the bathroom is america’s weirdest bathroom for sure. the urinal is inside the water closet (aka outhouse) and there is no bathtub as of now and either way there will be window treatments. its not an easy one to get or explain which is why i’m so excited to shoot it!

In a recent development, I thought tiles were rated for slipperiness…or maybe that’s only for tile that’s designated specifically for floors? I definitely remember checking that rating when we did our bathrooms.

Recent findings suggest that yes! Tiles have a DCOF (Dynamic Coefficient of Friction) rating that corresponds to slip risk. Depending on the tile’s DCOF there are recommended uses. For interior wet spaces you want to find a tile that has a wet DCOF of at least 0.42. Most tile manufacturers will also divide their tile offerings based on recommended use.

In a recent development, yes I knew about the DCOF but most tiles I love don’t indicate their rating. So I wasn’t sure if its a dated system. the higher end places will dictate if they can be for flooring but a lot of the more normal places don’t necessarily dictate. Flooring obviously needs to be way more durable than walls.

In a recent development, if you decide to go back to brick- we used to live in a house that had all brick floors (it was a passive solar design, and the brick really helped stabilize temperatures. I miss that house!). The brick is sealed, so it’s semi shiny and smooth, not rough at all on bare feet. It held up great in the kitchen and bath! I hear you on the “all reddish brown” challenge, but as a surface, brick can be great!

Oh wow. I would LOVE to see that house. I’ve never experienced a passive house before and sounds incredible. xx.

Sources indicate that so glad you moved away from the brick tile – pretty, but I agree with the downsides you mentioned. Just when I was feeling the gloss would be too shiny, you threw in the Ann Sacks enhancement at the end and I do really like that finish. The dark blue is a pretty color but may end up calling the color of the outhouse in question? But going too light wouldn’t be the right move either because it would be too high contrast. Also agree with some other posters’ comments, namely to pick tile that will withstand wear associated with outside debris like pebbles stuck in shoe treads etc, and also to pick grout color that won’t noticeably discolor over time from the outdoor foot traffic. Yes, you can seal the grout etc…but even frequent cleaning doesn’t seem to keep away the discoloration over time that occurs from outdoor traffic.

In a recent development, I have a glazed 2″x2″ tile in my bathroom and hate it. I can’t wait to change it out. The amount of grout is insane and so hard to keep clean. Also, my gut reaction to the textured tile is that -given that people will be using it from the outside- it that it’s going to be a nightmare to clean. Dirt will get imbedded into the textile and it won’t be easy to clean.

In a recent development, the grout thing is real – you NEED it for non-slip, but do yourself the biggest favor on earth and go mid-tone to dark with the grout!! It will hide any dirt brought in. I think it should be illegal to use white grout on floors. I have a medium gray in my high-traffic entry and it’s still lovely after 10 years (in spite of my very shoddy cleaning).

Sources indicate that agreed. I like a mid to dark tile grout for sure!

You do not want to take a risk with too slippery of floors, especially in a place where guests will frequent. This isn’t a “let’s test it out” kind of scenario.

All the examples you shared of glossier (satin to glossy) tile floors are bathrooms and mudrooms. These are places where people are expecting to be wet, changing footwear, wiping feet, and not passing through quickly or at all. These are also smaller spaces with rugs, benches and grab bars to help keep people from getting hurt and we all know, more or less, what to expect in bathrooms and mudrooms in terms of features and finishes. The predictability of risk helps us avoid problems.The cottage will have people, sometimes hurrying, in from a pool or lawn, wet shoes or bare feet sometimes. Having one fall wouldn’t be worth the risk to me- a concussion or broken hip, even bruised tailbone… . Personally, I really love the brick and the wood, and for a super old cottage rehab, I think it’s very appropriate too. You can also find a safer, less rustic floor tile if that’s your goal.

I agree – I do see that the contrast issue you are talking about but wouldn’t rugs help here… I would stay with the brick or something similar… looking forward to seeing which way you decide to go!

You make great points here ! Given all you said I’d be tempted to do retro lino!

I totally agree with Molly on this space being a large space used by a lot of people in a lot of different situations. That makes for a lot of different slip situations to consider. Follow Jessica’s advice about looking for the slip rating and be conservative in your choice. Also, having made houses safe for older parents, I can tell you that experts say to never use throw rugs/mats when making a space safe for older folks. Perhaps you could challenge yourself to find a great floor choice that sets a standard for stylish universal design, making it safe for the most vulnerable and/or disabled of your guests.

Recent findings suggest that would love that information. I’m remodeling and universal design is in the works. Have not got to flooring in primary bath that is significant enough for walker/wheelchair access. Flooring is critical here. The other bathrooms can have more “design” flooring.

I would worry about liquids getting into brick and smelling! IYKYK! What about a design with both shiny and flat tile?

It has been revealed that I am the Karen mentioned in your post above and my tiles were 6×6 tiles on the bathroom floor. It is a larger bathroom with tub and double vanity plus a separate water closet. Bath mat at the tub and two bathroom rugs at the vanity sinks. Stepping out of the tub the kids step on the bath mat and the next step had to be over to one of the rugs at the vanity. Any step on the tile with wet feet or dripping and making it wet, was a slip and slide situation. It also meant my elderly mom could not use that bathtub/shower because of the danger of slipping when wet. That tile was ripped out a week ago and now the bathroom has honed 12×24 marble look ceramic tile. Friction and less grout! It is a boring floor but I will be putting rugs down again and will style the counters with gorgeous accessories (that I can change out due to the boring colors I chose for the overall bathroom tiles, paint and polished nickel fixtures). You do you, I am function over form. Safety after not having it, was my priority. Check the DCOF of… Read more ».

Industry observers note that thank you Karen! i really appreciate the context and knowing that it was 6×6 tile. Really appreciate you weighing in here and being the inspiration for this post. Definitely taking your experience and wisdom in mind here. Thank you!

In a recent development, big thank you to this hugely relatable post! Thinking you found the thing, then wondering if something else was better, then all the safety questions, just, thank you for showing this side of the journey!

Sources indicate that I have glossy ceramic floor tile on the floors of both my bathroom and my guest bath (from Fireclay, if you want to look up the exact specs), and it has never caused me a moment’s worry. And this is coming from a chronic worrier and diagnosed anxious person.

I 100% agree. One knowledgeable rep remarked to me when wet glossy tiles are actually less slippery than Matt because feet stick more. Hence nearly all shopping malls have gloss floors! Not just for cleaning but for safety.

My mother had flat Matt ceramic 600x600mm in her kitchen and we all slipped on them when wet. Obviously with a texture this wouldn’t be the same concern.

In a recent development, I like the reflection of the space is small of a gloss. In my own bathrooms I used a lapatto finish (both gloss and matt with texture) Best of both worlds. Light reflecting and very grippy. I always recommend this finish to my clients for wet areas. I’m not a big fan of large grout areas to clean on my floors.

Recent findings suggest that OOH interesting!!!! That is such good insight. So maybe its very tile specific? Gah! going to look up Lapatto now, I don’t know that word so learning!

Well you can’t just show us a lovely Ann Sacks tile without telling us what color or collection it is! Don’t keep us in suspense!!

In a recent development, oh i wrote up there! Its the Made collection Provencal which has a texture (in slight gloss). More to come!

Industry observers note that who will be your “Rug Police”? Kids running about are not going to care about keeping them either dry or in place.

haha. I was going to choose vintage persian style rugs that generally are heavy enough (and with rug pads or rug tape) to not move. But I think we know the real answer is ME. I will be the rug police, lol.

Those rugs are going to get filthy if people are coming in here right from the outside.

Industry observers note that the rule about ceramic floor tiles is 4″ or smaller so that the grout prevent slipping. A 2×8 ceramic tile in herringbone pattern qualifies. Large format porcelain tile often has a wet floor version. If you do a glossy blue tile floor, I like the idea of 3×3 or 4×4 squares, just more contrast with the longer rectangular shapes of the wood. There was a trend in the 70s to put a glossy ultramarine blue tile with redwood walls – that could be fun! I’m sure whatever you decide will be gorgeous.

OOh thank you Christa! that is helpful (and hopeful). xx.

I’m still rooting for marmoleum—eco-friendly, vintage flair, easy-to-clean, and millions of colors and design options.

Recent findings suggest that also team marmoleum here! I put sage-colored marmoleum in a log cabin bathroom and LOVE it. It’s such a soothing sound underfoot.

I’m okay with more risks than most parents, but slips and falls on wet tile are not worth it, especially in a space frequented by guests.

This is very interesting and I haven’t thought of it!! It would be awesome in a more contemporary application. I have a weird philosophy (this is just a personal preference) that I don’t like to put hard finishes into a house that were invented after the era of the house was built. Mostly flooring and tile, cabinet style. Lighting and wallpaper don’t count but anything tied to the architecture of the house I like it to feel like it could have been the original XYZ (this also prevents me from using something too trendy and regretting it). Now i’ve broken this before, but its just something that is in the back of my head and its not a firm rule at all. But this material feels pretty contemporary so I’d be nervous that it would date the house. BUT BUT BUT BUT its awesome and cool and has a lot of pattern and color possibilities and boy does it check all the other boxes (safety, easy to clean) and I’ve never used it before so I’d learn something new. this house is also a house I’m not taking too seriously and trying to just have fun in and this material… Read more ».

Industry observers note that linoleum was invented in the 1860s. Using a modern version of it doesn’t seem much different from using a modern tile in a modern color.

Real linoleum like Marmoleum is a historically appropriate material.

Recent findings suggest that I also want hard finishes to be consistent with the age of a house. My house was built in 1938 and when I put a marmoleum/linoleum floor in my kitchen I was replacing an original linoleum floor. Also, marmoleum/linoleum has several practical advantages for kitchens and bathrooms that I have not seen in the comments here. It is naturally anti-microbial. If it gets an unsightly stain it can be sanded down to remove the stain because the color goes all the way through it. If it is damaged, the damage can almost always be fixed in a way that does not show. It comes in a lot of colors (maybe use a color that is in the stained glass door panel?). It comes in sheets and in click-together flooring options. It can be made shiny with the sealer. My floor is 22 years old. It still looks great and I still am so glad that I chose it.

Respectfully, skylights are not period appropriate.

Another thumbs up for Marmoleum. We put it in our mudroom/laundry in 2009 and it still looks great and is such a nice (and environmentally friendly) material. We live in the PNW with just a crawl space under our floor and we found the existing tile in the mudroom so cold – and wood seemed too risky. Then we found marmoleum and it was perfect. And yeah, marmoleum is just a brand of linoleum – which is absolutely appropriate for a house this age. Read the history here: (remove the spaces): www. hagley.org/ librarynews/ evolution-linoleum*.

I recently used waterproof marmoleum in my kids bathroom and we love it-quiet, soft and warm underfoot, easy to clean (no grout), naturally antimicrobial. And colorful! We used a light blue with green undertones. Honestly would like to replace all my tile with marmoleum.

I keep rooting for marmoleum somewhere in the “cottage” and the bathroom could be the perfect spot! I love it in our bathroom, where we did a simple old school checkerboard.

Industry observers note that porous brick in a bathroom is a significant NO for the ick reasons. I still don’t like shiny/slippery tiles regardless of size, and would always go honed and/or textured for better safety.

In a recent development, since the space is designated as a fun space, and you’re in Portland, why not do a fun recycled tiled floor. I’ve been to a few homes where at the party people want to hang in The bathroom , Marveling at all the fun details. Just order a bunch of boxes of fun new and vintage tiles and make it a conversation piece!

In a recent development, yes! I’ve thought about that a lot and its such a good idea. I don’t feel confidant in its execution but its SUCH a fun idea and if executed well would be 100% worth it.

That’s an incredible suggestion!

Don’t rely on rugs if you seriously envision this as a future home for seniors. Rugs present a tripping hazard and make it more difficult to move with wheelchairs or walkers.

According to recent reports, have you thought about tomettes? It’s quite French, so maybe too far from the look you’re going for, but they do have an old-world feel and they seem to stand the test of time. Just a thought!

It has been revealed that we have glossy ceramic tiles in our two main bathrooms and have not had any slipping incidents, even with three kids. I think thick enough grout lines are the key.

Sources indicate that love the Ann Sacks tile. Only other suggestion I had was to do a mix; mostly matte with random gloss of the same color mixed into the pattern. It’s a funky, eclectic look but it may work with the vibe of the space, since you’re going a bit funky in there already.

I just don’t think that tile fits the vibe of the guest house at all?? What about grout-less checkerboard “tile” of some sort? Same colors as on your sunroom floor? I know they make a high quality “tile” that isn’t really tile for the floor. Actually more expensive than doing hardwoods when I looked into doing it in my kitchen. Just a thought. Wish I could remember the name. But there were quite a few brands ands price points. They looked great in person.

I LOVE the idea of going with glossy small-scale floor tile in there for all the reasons you described… my favorite reason is to balance out the rustic warm walls with a little shiny contrast. But still not too distracting from the stained glass moment. I do suspect (as you did) that the slippery concern was primarily related to the large format tile. I think the texture of the grout lines will help a lot. I am just about to put in a 2” hex tile in the floor of our mountain cabin. Like you, we have tongue and groove walls in a warm st It’s quite bold for me in a glossy rusty red, but I’m going to tame it with a dark.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Regal” would be the word we’re going for this Thanksgiving.
  • Bread Plate | Rattan Charger | Dinner Plate | Paisley Napkin | Salad Plate | Goblet | Turkey Place Card Holders.
  • It has been revealed that the dishes are the stars (both meanings apply — grab Chris’s recipes here), so everything else plays a supporting role, except the brass bird.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Regal” would be the word we’re going for this Thanksgiving. We found these Spode Thanksgiving plates at Wayfair, and you just know the girls will call dibs. “I want the fox!” “I want the horse!” Someone will forever be the hound dog. It’s going to be a core memory (we hope!). To set the table, we grabbed some woven rattan chargers to make the plates pop without clashing, and a napkin layered between the dinner and salad plates turned everything a bit dressy. Is the dress code formal this year? It just might be!

Bread Plate | Rattan Charger | Dinner Plate | Paisley Napkin | Salad Plate | Goblet | Turkey Place Card Holders.

It has been revealed that the dishes are the stars (both meanings apply — grab Chris’s recipes here), so everything else plays a supporting role, except the brass bird. You don’t need fresh everything for Thanksgiving every year, but it’s good to have one thing that keeps coming back. He’s the one that’ll get saved. Pardoned. (Sorry. Had to.).

The dinnerware set comes with dinner, salad, and bread plates, and none of them scream Thanksgiving. Turkey salad plates were an option, but we went with one of every animal instead, about 20 in all, with no repeats. There are pheasants, rabbits, a hound dog, a horse, and a fox. It’s an instant conversation starter (“Oh, you’re at the fox seat”), and that kind of detail is exactly what nostalgia is made of.

Recent findings suggest that the rattan chargers were on our summer table. The silverware is our everyday set, and a great goblet works in any season. The splurge was the paisley linen napkins. They were bought for the occasion, but they’ll show up at every special dinner, which makes them a better buy than holiday napkins that sit in a bin 11 months a year. One simple trick: a napkin wrapped around a bottle of sparkling cider makes it feel like fine dining.

Add your email and we'll send you this post, so it's waiting for you whenever you're ready to dig in.

According to recent reports, when guests arrive, the first thing they’ll ask is where to sit. “Wherever you want” just leaves them feeling conflicted. Think about who’s coming and who will have the best conversations, then give everyone a spot. Sometimes you just have to lean into the theme with turkey place card holders, each finished with a ribboned gift tag and handwritten names. Bonus: guests can take the tags home, and they’re a sweet nod to the holidays ahead.

Recent findings suggest that christmas and Halloween both have decorations that come out year after year, and Thanksgiving deserves one too. Lots of families serve Thanksgiving dinner buffet-style, which leaves room on the table for a statement piece. Our brass bird is one of the only Thanksgiving-specific pieces here, so spending a little more on him is easy to justify. (Thinking about what we spend on a nice Christmas tree as an example!).

In a recent development, this is the easiest, most budget-friendly update there is. Change your tapers and ribbon for each holiday and keep everything else the same. These Wayfair tapers are in the color Portobello, a brown that ties all the tones into the royal blue tablecloth. They’re dripless, they burn for a long time (which you want for a long dinner), and they come in lots of colors. Next year, a upcoming tablecloth and a new taper color will give the same table a whole new look.

Pick your animal, pull up a chair, and shop everything we got from Wayfair to set this whole table below:.

    #47. The Best Gifts For Parents And Grandparents (How Do We Know? We Asked Ours:))

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2991 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Stylebyemilyhenderson ↗ Open Full Page

    The Best Gifts For Parents And Grandparents (How Do We Know? We Asked Ours:))

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Stylebyemilyhenderson

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that finding gifts for parents is so, so, so, so hard, and this year I spent hours texting them, begging for insight, then finding the solutions to their woes, and they DELIVERED.
    • According to recent reports, even if they don’t want more stuff (practical or not), I love sentimental and personal gifts, so finding really new and clever ones is a hobby for me.
    • According to recent reports, custom Family Recipe Book: I would LOVE this, and I know that any parent with a lot of family recipes would enjoy locking them in permanently.Jumbo Photo Playing Cards: GAH!
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that finding gifts for parents is so, so, so, so hard, and this year I spent hours texting them, begging for insight, then finding the solutions to their woes, and they DELIVERED. Outside of more time with us, their grandkids, and unique life experiences, they don’t really want to spend money on stuff. I like to do something personal and sentimental (photobook), and we usually do plan tickets to visit us. But outside of that, I get stumped. And yet they need certain things to make their lives more enjoyable and easier. I polled my mom and dad, Brian’s parents, and, of course, Jess had her dad (the famous Les) contribute as well. So most of these are coming from the source, with some extra ideas that I added in because I can see their pain points and just love practical ideas. Head over to the shop page if you want to just shop with fewer testimonials!

    According to recent reports, even if they don’t want more stuff (practical or not), I love sentimental and personal gifts, so finding really new and clever ones is a hobby for me. I would love any of these, personally.

    According to recent reports, custom Family Recipe Book: I would LOVE this, and I know that any parent with a lot of family recipes would enjoy locking them in permanently.Jumbo Photo Playing Cards: GAH! Imagine them showing up to their club with these cards!

    Custom Felted Family Portrait: So sweet (especially when you add any family pets in there).Personalized Embroidered Photo: Take a sweet photo of a trip or fun memory, and this artist will make it so special.Digital Frame: Get them a digital frame and preload it with all their favorite memories.

    Recent findings suggest that personalized Puzzle: Something to do, but make it feel special.Custom Photo Magnets: So stinking cute!! Imagine your fridge covered in these.

    Sources indicate that battery Organizer: Stock them up on batteries and put them in this case. No one wants to buy batteries!! Great housewarming gift, too. I want this. Motion-Detecting Smart Bulbs: So they don’t have to try to find the light switch in the middle of the night. Can be programmed easily (great for hallways or a lamp in the bathroom).

    According to recent reports, portable Extra Power Inverter: Jess’ dad, Les, recommended this – A great power bank that you can use with regular household cords. Great if you get stranded and need power! It is compatible with the DeWalt 20V battery. It allows you to have power for a regular 110v appliance. Comes in handy when you’re camping or even if you’re stuck in your car somewhere in the middle of nowhere. Most fresh cars have 110v outlets in them, but our old cars and trucks certainly do not. You won’t know how valuable this gadget is until you need it. That’s the day your guy will be thinking how perfect YOU are.Battery Operated Chainsaw: Sounds terrifying, but my dad wants this to keep their trees trimmed without hiring out, but he states so much easier to use than clippers. Also looks like fun.

    Label Maker: This is my mom’s favorite label maker. Very easy to use from an app on your phone. (In MY cart right now)Tool Set With Power Drill: A Les rec – Here is a small, handy dandy tool set from Deko. It is not as cheesy as most of these sets are. I don’t recommend it as a main tool set, but it is perfect to have in your vehicle. It has everything one might need in a pinch, and it doesn’t take up any space. It even has a cordless drill. (I just bought this to keep in our house; our tool room is INSANE).

    According to recent reports, two openers – one from Les (Jess’ dad), one from my mom. Sounds like a great gift idea if two of our parents love it, right?

    Industry observers note that elitra Home 3-in-1 Under-Cabinet Can Opener: Make cooking easier and faster. This is an electric can opener, blade sharpener, and bottle opener that mounts under your shelf.RoboTwist Automatic Jar Opener: It adjusts to whatever size jar you need to open (and is the most popular version).

    It has been revealed that ove Glove Set: My mom stated this oven mitt changed how she cooked in her kitchen. She loves it. Les (and Arlyn) have recommended this in the past!Brass Dishwasher Marker: The cutest brass dishwasher marker so you don’t have to wonder.

    Mason Jar Vacuum Sealer: My mom asked for this to help preserve leftovers. Think about it: when you are cooking for a small household (1-2 people), you have more leftovers that you want to preserve. This is SUCH a great gift to keep food lasting as long as possible. Onion Holder: Extra long. My mom has this and loves it. Makes it easier, safer, and more consistent to cook onions (I want this).

    Industry observers note that double Glasses Leather Case: This is SUCH a great gift for those of us who need both readers (or any seeing-eye glasses) and sunglasses. It has two pouches so you don’t have to carry around two separate cases and keeps them both protected. Glasses Cleaner: Brian’s mom indicates this is the best glasses cleaner, and I tested it out and agreed. A fun, little affordable gadget for anyone who has glasses.

    Kitchen Standing Mat: This is so much easier on their backs when standing to do the dishes. This one looks really nice, is easy to wipe up, and has a lot of cushioning (comes in other patterns and colors, too). Personalized Tissue Box!!: Comes in a lot of colors, and you order it with their names (or grandparent nicknames) on it for a personal touch. Practical and sentimental.

    Back Massager and Warmer: Think of all the hours of watching TV while getting massaged.Hand Massager: This is meant to be specifically great for arthritis, but I literally don’t know anyone who doesn’t love a hand massage.

    Warming Slippers: Oh geez. Put this in the microwave and then on your feet. HEAVEN.Beautyrest Heated Blanket: This one is big enough for bed and not full of faux fur (so more lightweight but still warm). I love this one for a smaller version for the sofa.

    Moccasin Slippers: They likely won’t splurge on these, but we can!Cowboy Western Slippers: From Les – It looks like you’re wearing cowboy boots, but they are actually slippers. Great idea for us older guys who do not want to look like an old man stumbling around in slippers. Ha!

    Jess’ dad, Les, put both of these on the list. Here are his personal reviews on them.

    Industry observers note that auto Pour-Over Coffee Maker: I bought a Breville Spiral Luxe pour-over coffee maker. Now, it’s a little pricey, but it’s quick, easy, and small. Hate a cluttered counter. When I’m cooking, it gets pretty cluttered, but when I’m not, I like it neat. One would never know I’m any good in the kitchen. I like it that way.Espro Go Po Insulated French press coffee maker: Also, for my long drives, I found this press coffee maker. Nothin’ like having hot coffee for the entire drive. Comes in multiple colors to fit your taste. I like that also.

    Magnetic Chess Set: We have this and love it. Its not specifically for travel, but so easy to bring anywhere. Emily Lex Watercolor Paint Set: Les Rec – I came across this watercolor paint set with a watercolor workbook. Basically, it is a paint-by-numbers set which I found to be quite relaxing and fulfilling. Shocking to me, actually, but great. The workbook comes in many different categories, from dogs to gardens. She even has notecards you can paint. One of those tremendous but simple ideas. Maybe my favorite thing on this list.NYT Puzzle Book: This book not only looks great, but is full of fun puzzles to keep the mind sharp.

    Sources indicate that hori Hori Knife: If you’re going to invest in one piece, this should be it. A hori hori knife can saw, dig, cut, and more. 10/10, highly recommended.Gardening Stool: This one is a seat, but also has easy storage and comes with a lot of tools. 40-Cell Seed Starter Tray: From my mom’s wish list (She has it now, but they are huge gardening enthusiasts).

    Sources indicate that garden Kneeler: Both my parents love this as avid gardeners. Super easy to move around, fold and unfold and can be used to kneel or sit. Garden Clogs: Super comfortable and durable!

    Another couple gift recs from Les.

    It has been revealed that dock Plus 4″x6″ Photo Printer: Kodak has a small photo printer. It is the retro 4×6-inch PD 460. You just dock your iPhone to it, and it will print your cowboy’s photo. Easy Peasy.Clip-on Bluetooth DeWalt Belt Speaker: If your parent likes music while they work, it is perfect. Nothin like whistlin’ while you work. (Did you know you can’t whistle and be miserable at the same time?) I keep finding all of these gadgets for the working man or woman. It just dawned on me that I spend way too much time in hardware stores. Yikes!

    XL Pill Box: These are meant to be the best pill boxes, customizable and come in a lot of sizes.Hydrogen Water Machine: My parents love theirs (and they are in great health). Definitely not mainstream yet, but research says fantastic for longevity.

    Industry observers note that ISDIN Age Contour: Suz influenced me (her skin is so fantastic for being 80), and I’ve been using this brand for the last three years and love it. ISDIN Flavo-C Serum Ampoules: This is such a great vitamin C oil. I use it day and night (when I remember), and it’s a noticeable difference on my skin. ISDIN Vitamin C Serum: From Suz: I use it in the AM & PM before applying moisturizer.

    Micro-Infusion Facial System: “Little vials that have tiny little needles; you apply serum all over the face. Really notice a difference. Puffs up fine lines. Only drawback is how difficult it is to open vials, and you can’t go in the sun for 12 hours after.”Dynamic Skin Recovery: My Mother-in-Law’s daily moisturizer (after the serum).Dermalogica Super Rich Repair: I use this every night before bed (extremely moisturizing).

    Tarte Shape Eye Concealer: “I use this to cover my dark circles”Tartelette Tubing Mascara: “It stayed on through 18 holes of golf with wind making eyes tear up.”Celor Under Eye Patches: “I have major dark circles under my eyes. If they’re really bad, I use these”.

    Slip-on Shoes: Slip on while standing and all-day comfort (great for errands or around the house chores).Soft Lounge Sleep Set: Incredibly soft and perfectly draped pajamas that are very Emily Henderson-approved.

    Packable Goose Down Jacket: So lightweight and warm, it feels like you are wearing nothing but still so warm. Great for long walks.Heated Vest: Again, I think this gift guide is for me. Comes in parkas, too.Heated Gloves: Wow. Such a great gift for anyone in the winter, up north or not.

    It has been revealed that let me make a suggestion in the blue jean world. Usually when a guy finds a pair of jeans that he likes and fits well he will stick with them forever. I was that guy. Then I stumbled onto a pair of Hudson jeans, and I was sold. They fit well and wear well. They are soft and a little stretchy. Can’t beat ‘em. In my cowboy days (yep, a real cowboy), I wore Wranglers cause that’s just what you did. They were always rather stiff, but that is what cowboys wore. Lo and behold, Wrangler has just come out with a jean called Toughlite™ Cowboy Cut® Slim Fit Jean. That makes all the sense in the world to me. Gotta wonder why they took so long. Throw in a cowboy hat, and it’s time to take a picture. Also, let’s not forget the jean jacket. Classic and timeless!

    In a recent development, toto Bidet Toilet Seat: I don’t know. Just seems like what every grown-up I know is swearing about right now. Airplane Seat Cushion: Jess’ dad Les Rec – As you guys know, I have a cabin near South Lake Tahoe. It is only a three-hour drive or less, yet my bony butt still gets sore from the drive. Solved that problem with the Travel Comfort Kit. It’s an inflatable seat cushion for long drives or long flights. It has sure made my butt much happier on my journeys. Nothin’ worse than a sore ass during a trip that is supposed to be a pleasant experience. The thing folds up into a pouch when not in use. Sure came in handy.Portable Stadium Seat: Portable for all the Little League games they come to (10k reviews with a 5-star rating).

    Recent findings suggest that monogrammed Golf Ball Marker: I got these for Brian’s dad last year, and it’s such a fun little personalized gift. Golf Pencils: Les Rec – Years ago I bought a box of small pencils like the ones you see at a golf course. I have never been tasked with looking for a pencil since then. What a relief. It’s a small, inexpensive gift that your parent doesn’t even know they need or want. I guarantee they will be calling you to thank you on more than one occasion (with apologies for the weird look he gave you when he opened them). I cannot tell you how many times I have set a pencil down and the universe ate it. Make sure they have erasers. Once in a while, even we make mistakes.White Handkerchiefs: Les Rec – I am a handkerchief guy. I have always carried one, mainly because my Dad did. It seems to be a lost habit. Someone just gifted me a box of them, and I loved it. You can pick from many brands on Amazon. I prefer the soft cotton variety.

    Recent findings suggest that life 360 Tracking Device: Great for phone, wallets, and keys (anything really) tracked through the same program. Or if you just want to keep an eye on where everyone is. Apple AirTags: They are annoying to buy, but my goodness, so practical to have (we love ours).

    Acupressure Back Relief Pillow: These are a little gentler than the acupressure mats and still great for back pain.Neck AC: I bought this for myself, and it’s simple, works, and would be a great gift for walking or golfing in the heat.

    I hope this is as helpful to you as it is to all of us. Finding those gifts for our parents and grandparents can feel so impossible, but not with this list, stacked with personal recs from our favorite parents and grandparents:) Again, head to the shop page for everyone on your list!

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    *This post is in partnership with Sézane but all opinions are my own.

    Recent findings suggest that I have amassed quite a collection of outdoor furniture over the years. Much of it is secondhand, pieces I’ve picked up at thrift stores or found on Facebook Marketplace. There is less concrete to cover with seating in this backyard than there was at our last house, but I still love so many of the sets and wanted to hold onto them. Instead of keeping it all near the house, I thought it would be fun to tuck tables and chairs and benches into the woods.

    This little set with the Greek key details could probably use a paint job, but I don’t mind the chippy look. It allows it to stand out in the midst of all of the green without being too high contrast. One of the reasons I thought it would be fun to place seating throughout Three Pastures was to encourage rest. To give reason for slowing down, taking a seat, and enjoying the landscape. By nature I want to “do,” and there is so much to be done when you live on land. But this calls us to sit, connect, reflect.

    In a recent development, sézane is one of my favorite clothing brands, and I had no idea they also had a home line. (The lamps are out of this word!) I picked a few pieces that are perfect for a relaxing afternoon in the shade.

    DRESS | JACKET | TABLECLOTH | PILLOW | PLATES | PITCHER.

    I have a few more sets to place, but I’m loving the surprises amongst the trees. Have you ever placed outdoor furniture like this? Do you use it?

    #36. How to Style a Holiday Mantel

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1063 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Chrislovesjulia ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Style a Holiday Mantel

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Chrislovesjulia

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that we decorate our entire house for Christmas, but the living room is really the star of the show.
    • It has been revealed that we’ve styled our mantel in different ways over the years and have landed on a formula for foolproof mantel styling.
    • We always start with faux greenery, and our go-to is cedar — we love the airy look of the branches and the texture of the needles.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that we decorate our entire house for Christmas, but the living room is really the star of the show. It’s where the big tree goes, where our girls open their presents on Christmas morning, and where we entertain guests over the holidays. While the tree commands a lot of attention, the true focal point of the room is the fireplace. It’s the obvious spot for the stockings, but it’s also a great canvas for adding greenery and other styling elements to make the room feel like the holidays. Here’s the formula we come back to every year, plus a look back at our last three mantels.

    It has been revealed that we’ve styled our mantel in different ways over the years and have landed on a formula for foolproof mantel styling. Here’s how it comes together.

    We always start with faux greenery, and our go-to is cedar — we love the airy look of the branches and the texture of the needles. Whatever garland you use, make sure it’s longer than your mantel so you have room for the swags and some to hang off each side. Some people drape garland straight across the mantel, but we like to let it swag down on both sides. This way, the garland stays visible and you leave room for other styling elements on the surface of the mantel.

    A versatile and budget-friendly option for a 9′ cedar garland.

    Next, add something to give your greenery interest. Maybe that’s more greenery in a different texture, like a mixed eucalyptus or pine. Other options include beaded garland, brass bells, dried orange slice garlands, or even something unique like the brass “Merry Christmas” banner we’ve used in the past. This is also the step where you’d add lights, if you want them. We typically leave lights out of our garland, preferring candlelight and other ambient light, but they’re a great option if you’re looking for some extra sparkle.

    Sources indicate that it’s no secret that we love a holiday bow, and the mantel is no exception. Every styling moment needs a focal point, and we like to use a large bow in the center to pull everything together. A lot of our holiday decor gets reused and repurposed around the house year after year, so we change up the ribbon color to keep things feeling fresh.

    If you’re not confident hand tying bows there are tons of pre-made tree topper options out there that would work beautifully on a mantle.

    It’s easy to overdo the top of the mantel and take away from the moment you’ve created with the garland, but really all you need is a little height on one or both sides to balance the visual weight of the garland and stockings below. We like to use candlesticks for this, since they add height and ambiance in one move, but you can also use other things from around the house, like a vase full of greenery or even a piece of art on one side.

    There are many ways to hang stockings, and it really depends on the shape and structure of your mantel. We use small screw-in hooks on the underside of ours. The holes are barely visible the rest of the year and they look cleaner than stocking holders. You can go all matching with your stockings or mix and match patterns (we designed a collection made just for this!). We have a large family, so we typically put three on one side and two on the other. Just remember to place something vertical on the mantel diagonally across from your stockings so the visual weight feels even on both sides.

    Our Chris Loves Julia + Pottery Barn Kids collection of stockings come in 11 patterns that are made to mix and match.

    In a recent development, last year, our Christmas tree was to the left of the fireplace, so we opted to go a little lighter on the garland to avoid the greenery blending in with the tree. We layered a red beaded garland over the top with a large burgundy ribbon in the center (full permission to mix your red tones — it looks so refined). We hung the stockings just below the garland so the beads stayed the focus.

    Add your email and we'll send you this post, so it's waiting for you whenever you're ready to dig in.

    According to recent reports, instead of layering in beads or metal, this year we mixed greenery of different textures, like cedar and Norfolk pine. The result is a lush, botanical moment that needs little else besides some red ribbon for contrast.

    According to recent reports, this mantel plays with warm and cool tones — the silver ribbon layered with the brass “Merry Christmas” garland, the warm gold of the mirror contrasted with the cool-toned sage stockings underneath. A silver ribbon bow and tall tapers on both sides keep it feeling balanced and a little unexpected.

    Sources indicate that you rarely need just one garland for a mantel. They look best layered, with multiple strands of the same type or a mix of greenery for a fuller, more botanical look. If you’re following our formula, place one garland on either side of the bow at the center point — just make sure the branches point outward, not back toward the center.

    Sources indicate that we use Command hooks for ours — one in the center (where the bow usually goes) and one at each anchor point on the outer corners of the mantel. Because of the shape of our mantel, we hang our stockings from small screw-in hooks on the underside, but you can also use Command hooks or a weighted stocking holder like this one.

    Absolutely. Any long piece of furniture in your room, like a console table, dresser, or sideboard, can stand in for a mantel.

    StockingsTree Skirts & ToppersHoliday DecorGreeneryChristmas TreesAdvent CalendarsFrame TV ArtHoliday CardsOrnaments.

    Painted Ceramic Christmas Village Houses

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jenniferrizzo

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ceramic Christmas villages are a sweet addition to holiday decorating, they are also easy to find at thrift stores.
    • According to recent reports, this post contains affiliate links.
    • Sources indicate that in the 1980’s and 90’s, it seemed like a lot of households had these.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ceramic Christmas villages are a sweet addition to holiday decorating, they are also easy to find at thrift stores. Some times you can find them, but they don’t match, If you’re looking for a way to create a colorful and eclectic Christmas color palette , try using rainbow colors to create a painted ceramic Christmas village houses with fun and bright paints. For even more fun, use multi-purpose paint with a little sparkle in it. Old ceramic houses can be found for a few dollars each, and same for the paint. with 7 houses, this project can be expected to cost under $20, depending on how much the houses cost.

    According to recent reports, this post contains affiliate links. See our sponsor and affiliate disclosure here.

    Sources indicate that in the 1980’s and 90’s, it seemed like a lot of households had these. We had a neighbor that had 30 or 40, and would nestle her entire collection in faux snow under her tree. She also had a cement goose that sat on her front stoop that was super cute. She would dress it up for every holiday, including a bright yellow raincoat for rainy days… but that is an entirely other another story all together. Let’s get back to the ceramic houses. These houses aren’t actually from the same collection. I picked them up here and there at different visits to the thrift store. Some of them are even meant for a tealight. Since they are now painted, I will probably put a battery operated candle inside, or fairy lights. I started by  giving them a dusting and cleaning and removing some candle wax. Regular craft paint can be used, They aren’t going to get heavy use, so I’m not worried about chipping . Also, once these are painted only use fairy lights or battery operated candles in them. Even if they are made for it, don’t use real candles any more.

    Sources indicate that -Multi-purpose paint in a base color and a sparkle color or paintable glitter paint. We used DecoArt multi-surface and Glamour Dust paint.

    -Clear coat sealer -if using regular acrylic craft paint.

    -Primer or base coat of white paint.

    -Tarp or covering for the table.

    Started by putting on a layer of base coat of the multi-surface craft paint. on the houses and let dry. This may take 1 -2 coats for complete coverage. Let dry completely before moving onto the next step.

    It has been revealed that even though you can paint Glamour Dust Paint on it’s own, it’s really much more intense with a paint color underneath. By mixing and matching paints, you can make some really fun color combinations. I matched my acrylic paint as close as I could to my Glamour Dust paint to get a matte solid finish and cover up the detail on the house underneath. Let your acrylic paint dry completely before applying a layer of Glamour Dust. There’s a chart farther down in the post you can pin and save for later.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s kind of fun how painting something with acrylic paint makes it look different, like these trophies I painted a few years ago.The Glamour Dust is fun because it has a really fine glitter, so you get more of a matte, sparkly finish which is really pretty. It works best when applying thin coats, and letting them dry to build up a more glittery finish.

    I ended up with about 2 coats of acrylic paint, and 5 coats of Glamour Dust on each house by the time I was done.

    I used a craft foam brush in the beginning, and then I switched to a regular soft bristled brush. It worked much better to get in the cracks and crevices.

    Once they dried, they had such a pretty shimmer and sparkle.

    It was a fun to turn the village into a rainbow holiday decor!

    Industry observers note that up close you can really see the shimmer of the Glamour Dust. It’s so pretty in person!

    I put together a couple of charts so it’s easy to get the same look.

    Below is the printable version.

    Once my Christmas decor goes up, I am going to put my Rainbow Christmas Village on my mantel with Bottlebrush Trees, and some other fun holiday decor.
